tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

`/forecast-capture` skill, which snapshots predictions **before kickoff** and reports what
moved since the prior week.

  writes, so detection is unaffected.

Confirmed 2026-09-09. The Mac's `data/weekly_forecast_log.csv` looked like it had
missed 2026-08-26 and 2026-08-31 — it jumped 07-31 → 09-02. Neither week was
missed. **Both were captured on the Windows box**, which runs the same wrapper
against the same repo. The two machines had diverged, each holding captures the
other lacked.

Before declaring a missed week, check the other machine's copy of the log.
Merging is safe: the natural key is `(captured_at, season, team, week, game_id)`,
and a union on that key had **zero conflicts** across 216 Mac + 348 Windows rows
→ 540. Same key never carried different values. See [[github-consolidation]].

## An old newest-snapshot file is not proof of a missed week

Checked 2026-09-02: the newest snapshot was `2026-07-31_baylor.csv`, and both the skill and
COMMANDS.md asserted the 08-24 and 08-31 weeks were "gone for good". They were not — Baylor's
opener was 2026-09-05, so no game had been played and nothing had been overwritten. **A week
is lost only if a game was actually played inside the gap.** Verify before declaring a loss:

```
curl -s "https://site.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/football/college-football/teams/239/schedule?season=2026"
```

(239 = Baylor; read each event's `status.type.name`.) Both docs were corrected.

## Cadence

- ~~**Wednesdays**, season window **2026-08-26 → 2027-01-20**~~ — superseded
  2026-08-15. Current cadence is **Monday-anchored**, season window
  **2026-08-24 → 2027-01-23**. See "Cadence" below, which is authoritative.

## The constraint that makes the cadence non-negotiable

**There is no backfill.** A pre-game forecast is only capturable before the game is played;
a missed week is permanently missing from the series, not a chore that rolls
forward. This is why the reminder escalates rather than silently re-queuing.

## Mac-side guard (built 2026-08-15)

`ritual-check.ps1` now carries a fourth ritual, `forecast-capture`, so the cadence is
enforced on this machine rather than depending on memory. It detects captures from the
artifact itself — newest `*_baylor.csv` in `~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/data/weekly_snapshots/`
— matching the script's existing "the artifact is the record, not a state file" rule.

**The real deadline is Saturday's kickoffs, not a maintenance window.** The report
overwrites its Chance of Victory column with the realised result once a game is *played* —
that is what destroyed 2019–2025. Nothing scheduled updates midweek.

Cadence (Monday-anchored, per Eric 2026-08-15 — he wanted the warning early in the week):
**Mon DUE → Tue–Sat OVERDUE → Sun silent** (games played, week gone). Season bounds are the
Monday of the opening week (2026-08-24) and the Saturday of the closing week (2027-01-23),
widened from the documented 08-26 → 01-20 so neither end truncates a live capture window.

A third status, **RECHECK**, exists because an early capture is not proof of a good one: the
source may not have refreshed the coming weekend's numbers on Monday, so a Monday snapshot
can hold last week's figures. Treating "captured this week" as done would let a stale
snapshot pass for a good week — the exact risk that makes capturing early otherwise unsafe.
So a capture taken *earlier* in the week keeps surfacing through Wednesday. Capturing today
always satisfies today; RECHECK means *verify*, not *you missed it*.

Three counterintuitive silences (off-season, Sunday, post-Wednesday-once-captured) plus the
RECHECK window are pinned by `tests/keystone-ritual-forecast-capture.ps1`. Both a
days-since-last-capture and a naive "captured this week → OK" implementation fail them. The
script gained `-Today` and `-CfbSnapshotDir` seams to make this testable.

**`-Notify` was mute on this Mac from the migration until 2026-08-15** — it shelled out to
`msg.exe` (Windows-only), so every scheduled run hit the catch and logged "desktop prompt
unavailable" where nobody reads it. Now `osascript`, dialog with a banner fallback. This
affected *all* rituals, which is consistent with interview-me sitting 12 days overdue and
weekly-review 15. If ritual nags ever go quiet again, test `-Notify` directly before
assuming the rituals are simply current.

Schedule: `com.keystone.rituals` fires Mon–Fri 17:00 plus Fri 15:30, so Monday's DUE and the
Tue–Fri escalation all land. **Saturday and Sunday have no trigger** — Saturday's OVERDUE is
therefore only visible if the script is run by hand. Acceptable because Fri 15:30 and 17:00
are the last useful warnings anyway, but it does mean the Saturday branch is effectively a
manual-run safety net, not a live alarm.

A Windows-side scheduled task `CFB-ForecastCaptureReminder` was left enabled when the
Windows box was retired 2026-08-14 — it operates under that machine's own `~/Desktop/DEV`
and touches none of the Mac repos, so it is harmless but is *not* the authoritative
reminder. See [[backup-sync-system]].

Related model/data work lives in [[cfb-analytics-lab]] (a separate project —
`~/DEV/CFB_Analytics_Lab` vs the Victory Model's own tree).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/forecast-capture

# Forecast Capture

Freezes cfbvictorymodel.com's forecasts for the coming weekend, then reports
what changed. Takes no arguments and asks nothing — all 16 Big 12 teams and
2026 are the defaults and rarely change.

## Why this exists

The report's "Chance of Victory" column is **overwritten with the realised
result** once a game is played. Across 2019–2025 that destroyed every pre-game
probability the model ever produced. Miss a week and that week's forecast is
gone permanently — it cannot be recovered later. This makes 2026 the first
gradable season.

## Run it

One command does everything — capture all 16 Big 12 teams, compare, and copy
both into the archive:

```bash
/Users/kristinarash/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/scripts/weekly_run.sh
```

That wrapper is the only route to run. It hardcodes the absolute `uv` path
(`/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/uv`) so it works from any shell, and it calls:

```bash
uv run --with playwright python weekly_capture.py            # default = all Big 12
uv run python compare_snapshots.py --all --archive
```

Pass through to narrow it — `scripts/weekly_run.sh --team Baylor` for one team,
`--year 2027` for another season.

Snapshots are written to `data/weekly_snapshots/` (canonical) and copied to
`~/DEV/CFB_Forecast_Archive/<season>/` together with each team's comparison
text. The archive is a read-only mirror; never treat it as the source.

Then read the comparison output back to the user in plain language (see below).

**Budget ~10 minutes.** Sixteen teams share one report session. This is a
hobby server run by one person — do not run it more often than weekly, and do
not add teams beyond the conference without a reason.

**Must run headed.** A Chrome window will open — that is expected, not a bug.
In headless mode Power BI's virtualised slicer list never renders past the
first ~8 alphabetical teams and most teams are unreachable. Do not add
`--headless`.

`Team attempt 1 failed, retrying...` in the output is **normal** — the first
slicer interaction races the app's own start-up. It retries 3×, and any team
still failing gets one whole extra pass at the end. Only treat it as a failure
if a team appears in the final `FAILED for:` line.

## What to report back

Lead with how many of the 16 teams captured, then give the rollup table
`compare_snapshots.py --all` prints (team, expected wins, change, played,
moved). Then:

1. **Games played since last capture** — the forecast is now gradable for
   those. Report side correct/wrong and margin miss. This is the accumulating
   track record; it is the whole point.
2. **Forecasts that moved** — which games and by how much. A big win-probability
   swing usually means the model re-rated an opponent after their weekend.
3. **Season outlook drift** — expected wins now vs last week.
4. **Anything anomalous** — a new game appearing, a game vanishing, fewer than
   12 rows, or a wild swing worth a second look.

Keep it short. If nothing moved, say so in one line.

## Timing

Run **Wednesday** of a game week. Wednesday sits after the model has ingested
the previous weekend and safely before Thursday-night kickoffs. Monday risks
catching the model mid-update; Friday risks missing a Thursday game.

If the comparison output warns the newest capture is several days old, tell the
user which week was missed — that forecast is unrecoverable and the gap should
be recorded rather than quietly ignored.

## Which machine

**The Mac owns the weekly capture (decided 2026-09-23).** On Windows, do not run
it — stop and tell the user. On 9/23 both machines captured Baylor, and the sync
merge conflicted on `data/weekly_forecast_log.csv` and that day's snapshot.

## Which teams

The default is the whole Big 12 — all 16, every week. The list lives in one
place, `BIG12` in `weekly_capture.py`. Edit that constant if the conference
changes; do not scatter team lists into the wrapper or this file.

Outside the Big 12, only if asked. Each extra team is another slow slicer set
against one person's hobby server:

```bash
scripts/weekly_run.sh --teams Baylor TCU "Texas Tech"
```

Team names must match the report's Team slicer exactly — "Iowa State", not
"Iowa St."; "UCF", not "Central Florida". A wrong name fails loudly with
`never appeared (saw [...])` and that message lists what the slicer really
offers, so read it rather than guessing again.

## Gotchas

- **`playwright` is not installed on any Python on this machine.** `weekly_capture.py`
  imports it, so the bare `python3 weekly_capture.py` form this skill documented until
  2026-09-02 dies with `ModuleNotFoundError` before opening a browser. `uv run --with
  playwright` fetches it per-run (~12ms, cached). Never remove `--with playwright` from
  the run block. `compare_snapshots.py` is stdlib-only and does not need it.
- **The browser cache is separate from the Python package.** A `ModuleNotFoundError` is
  never a reason to re-download browsers. But `uv run --with playwright` pulls the newest
  playwright, and each release wants its own build under `~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/`.
  On 2026-09-23 it jumped from `chromium-1234` to `chromium-1243` and the capture died
  with `Executable doesn't exist at .../chromium-1243/...`. Fix, then re-run:
  `uv run --with playwright python -m playwright install chromium` (~95 MB).
- **Check what already exists before capturing.** `ls data/weekly_snapshots/` first. On

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.

- **Registry drift.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It compares `portfolio.json` with every DEV folder and Drive `01_PROJECTS` folder and only reports; it never moves anything. Do not fix drift during closeout. List each item it found under "Still open", naming any folder created this session first: that is a project started without a row, the exact way projects got lost before the 2026-10-03 organization pass. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran; say so, do not call it clean. Cowork cannot run it; say it was skipped.
- **7-day rule.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name any project it paused, and any project on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it still needs (a receiver, step 1). Revive with the board's status pill or `portfolio.py` once there is a first step to show.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

- **Registry edits get their own commit.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json` shows a change (board edits from the day, `set-status`, `set-receiver`), commit that file alone first as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`, then the rest. The board header's "N unpushed registry edits" counts these; a skipped one becomes a JSON merge conflict when the other machine edits too.
- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- If `~/.claude/mods` changed this session (a mod added, edited or `.disabled`), run the mods sync (`bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` on the Mac, `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` on Windows) and list any invalid mod under "Still open".
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- **Deliverables.** A finished file made for someone else this session (PDF, deck, report, sheet) gets a copy at `~/DEV/_DRIVE/03_REPORTS/YYYY-MM-DD_<Sport>_<Topic>_<Audience>.<ext>`. The repo keeps the source; Drive keeps the handed-off copy. Name the copy in the report.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log`. If not empty, surface it and fix the hook issue if obvious, then append its lines to `transcripts/.errors.log.archived-<YYYY-MM-DD>` and clear it with `cp /dev/null` (same archive-then-clear step as backup and claude-stack-doctor; `: > file` is dcg-blocked).
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

- `## Next` — most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to open), not a theme: it is the line `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows Eric the next morning
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric, each one written out in full as its own top-level bullet: the question itself and enough context to answer it without opening another file. - `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

Then run `python ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --decisions --days 1`. It prints exactly what tomorrow's `/startup` will show as "Decisions waiting on you". Every decision this session left open must appear there as a readable question; if one is missing or shows as a pointer, fix that repo's `## Open questions` before the commit.

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

**Keep the resume cards true (PM system design Decision 9).** The live board shows each project as a card read from STATUS and the registry; if a card doesn't make sense tonight, it won't in six weeks. Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (about a minute), then `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. It prints the card of every registry project touched today, on either machine, with its gaps. Fix each gap before the Step 2 commit:

- `STATUS has no entry dated <today>`: add `- <today>: <what happened>` under the repo's Done / Current state.
- `STATUS has no Next item`: put one concrete action first under `## Next`.
- `no next step (next_action)` (Drive-only row): set it on the board or with `portfolio.py add-update <name> "<note>" --next-action "<step>"`.
- `needs a receiver`: `portfolio.py set-receiver <name> "<who>"` (a name, or `me: <why>`). Ask Eric when it is not obvious from the session; never invent one.
- `touched but marked <status>`: revive it (`portfolio.py set-status <name> active`) or say in STATUS why a retired project was touched.

Re-run `card-check` after the fixes. Its output is the last section of the report (**Cards:**); trim to projects with work today if it is long, but never drop one that still has a gap.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none"> (`portfolio.py crosswalk`)
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.

**Cards:** <`portfolio.py card-check` output, after the Step 4 fixes>
```

The cards come last on purpose: they are what the next session, on either machine, picks up from.

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

**Where everything landed.** Build that list from the ledger, not from memory: the Step 4 `landed.py scan --days 1` already refreshed it (it reads git in every DEV repo and file times on Drive and the vault, so files written by scripts and shell copies are included); run `landed.py show --days 1`. Put its project-grouped output in the report under **Landed:** (trim to the projects this session touched if it is long). The ledger lives in `~/.claude/global-memory/landed/` and is pushed with global-memory, so `/landed` on the other machine shows it too.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# 2026-10-23 — Big 12 capture (late week), site found stale

## What and why
Eric asked whether "weekly-capture" was broken. There is no skill by that name; the
skill is `/forecast-capture` (its script is `weekly_capture.py`). The skill works, but the
Wednesday 10-21 run had been missed. Ran it Friday 10-23, before Saturday's kickoffs.

## Result
- 16/16 Big 12 teams captured, no failures. `scripts/weekly_run.sh`, exit 0.
- No forecast lost: ESPN scoreboard (group 4) shows no Big 12 games on Thu 10-22 or Fri 10-23.
- **cfbvictorymodel.com is stale.** Every 10-23 snapshot matches 10-14 except `captured_at`.
  The site shows 4 Baylor games played; ESPN shows 6 (ASU 10-04 and TCU 10-17 missing).
  The model has not ingested results since about 9-27. The compare reported
  "No game was newly played and no forecast moved."

## Decision
Kept the capture even though it is unchanged: it is still the pre-game forecast the site
published before the 10-24 games, which is the only thing the series records.

skill is `/forecast-capture` (its script is `weekly_capture.py`). The skill works, but the

published before the 10-24 games, which is the only thing the series records.
